subject: pathology
title: Atherosclerosis, hypertension and aneurysms

steps.tx: Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease of large and medium arteries. A mature **atheroma** has a fibrous cap and a **necrotic lipid core** with cholesterol clefts and foam cells. Lesions begin as fatty streaks in youth, and decades later they complicate by rupture, erosion, aneurysm formation or stenosis.
steps.say: Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease of large and medium sized arteries. A mature plaque has a fibrous cap over a necrotic lipid core. Fatty streaks develop in youth and complications occur decades later in adults. Rupture and stenosis are important because they cause acute events.

vis.caption: Mature atheroma showing fibrous cap, necrotic lipid core, and key components. Image: Yang, Wen Jie; Fisher, Mark; Zheng, Lu; Niu, Chun Bo; Paganini-Hill, A, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

steps.tx: Endothelial injury allows lipid entry and triggers inflammation inside the arterial wall. **LDL oxidation** promotes foam cell formation, and the **fibrous cap** is laid down by smooth muscle cells. A thick cap with little inflammation is stable, whereas a thin cap with heavy inflammation is vulnerable to rupture.
steps.say: Endothelial dysfunction is important because it allows LDL entry into the intima. Oxidised lipid is taken up and macrophages become foam cells in the wall. Smooth muscle cells form the fibrous cap over the lipid core. Plaque stability is determined by cap thickness and inflammation.

right.title: Vulnerable plaque
points: Often only moderately stenotic before events

steps.tx: Plaque rupture exposes thrombogenic material and triggers rapid arterial occlusion. **Plaque rupture** causes thrombosis within minutes, and **plaque erosion** causes thrombosis without frank rupture in some patients. Healed silent ruptures add new layers to a plaque, and this process explains stepwise growth of stenosis over time.
steps.say: Plaque rupture exposes collagen and tissue factor to flowing blood rapidly. Thrombosis develops within minutes and it occludes the affected artery completely. Erosion is different because thrombosis occurs without frank cap rupture. Healed ruptures are layered and they increase stenosis gradually.

steps.tx: Hypertension damages arteries through sustained pressure and vascular remodelling. Benign hypertension causes **hyaline arteriolosclerosis**, and malignant hypertension causes **fibrinoid necrosis** with onion skin change in small vessels. Sustained pressure hypertrophies the left ventricle, and target organ damage affects the retina, kidney and brain in characteristic patterns.
steps.say: Hypertension injures vessels through sustained pressure and vascular remodelling over years. Hyaline change develops in benign disease and fibrinoid necrosis occurs in malignant disease. The left ventricle hypertrophies because it pumps against increased resistance chronically. The eyes, kidneys and brain show target organ damage.

steps.tx: An aneurysm is a permanent localised dilation caused by weakening of the arterial wall. An **abdominal aortic aneurysm** is usually atherosclerotic and infrarenal, and **rupture risk** rises steeply as diameter increases. Aortic dissection is different because blood splits the media through an intimal tear and creates a false lumen.
steps.say: An aneurysm is a permanent dilation and it is caused by wall weakening. The abdominal aorta is affected below the renal arteries most often. Rupture risk rises steeply because wall tension increases with diameter. Dissection is different because blood splits the media through a tear.

rows: All wall layers dilated but intact
Circle of Willis bifurcations; subarachnoid bleed

steps.tx: This contrast CT shows a large infrarenal aneurysm in coronal and axial views. The **aneurysm sac** is dilated, and **mural thrombus** lines the sac around the bright patent lumen. Recognising the infrarenal position matters because rupture risk and repair decisions are central examination topics for abdominal aortic aneurysm.
steps.say: This CT shows a dilated infrarenal aortic sac in two planes. The patent lumen is bright and mural thrombus lines the aneurysm sac. The renal arteries are shown above the aneurysm in the coronal view. Diameter is important because rupture risk rises steeply with size.
